newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico calls Salinas to give murder trial evidence.
newsitem.headline: Mexico calls Salinas to give murder trial evidence.

text.p: For the first time in modern Mexican history, a judge has summoned a former president to testify in a trial, Mexican media reported on Saturday.

Federal judge Ricardo Ojeda on Friday ordered former president Carlos Salinas to declare in the murder trial of his brother Raul Salinas, accused of masterminding the 1994 shooting of a top ruling party politician.
Salinas, who lives in self-imposed exile in Dublin, will not have to return to Mexico to appear in court. He can testify at the Mexican consulate in Ireland, the judge said.
The judge's summons came one day after prosecutors said Carlos Salinas knew his brother was suspected of masterminding the 1994 shooting but tried to get him off the hook.
The ruling breaks with a long-standing unwritten rule in Mexico that former presidents are "untouchable."
The Salinas family has always insisted that Raul, imprisoned in a maximum security jail since March 1995 on murder and illicit enrichment charges, is innocent.

Prosecutors believe Raul ordered the September 1994 murder of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, then secretary-general of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), because of a family feud. Ruiz Massieu was at the time divorced from Raul and Carlos's sister Adriana.
Judge Ojeda also called on Ruiz Massieu's brother, Mario, a former deputy attorney general, to give evidence at the upcoming trial, for which a date has still not been set.

Mario Ruiz Massieu is fighting extradition from the United States to face charges of obstruction of justice and embezzlement. He is currently under house arrest pending the repeated attempts to return him to Mexico.
"Testimony of Carlos Salinas de Gortari and Mario Ruiz Massieu are fundamental and necessary," the judge said.

Prosecutors presented new evidence this week including a cassette tape anonymously sent to prosecutors, in which one of a pair of brothers accused of helping in the murder said that Raul had ordered it.
Salinas denied interfering in a murder investigation to cover up his brother Raul's alleged involvement.

"Carlos Salinas de Gortari emphatically and firmly denies any insinuation that he may have intervened in the course of the investigation," the former president said in a statement issued by his lawyer.
